Give-back experience · Kids become the scientists

Thirty minutes in, the room finds out why it’s here.

Your people arrive expecting team building. They compete. They solve things. Then a locked object opens in front of them and the room goes quiet — because the message inside says the exercise was never the point. Children are on their way, and each team has minutes to figure out how to inspire one of them. One program, ninety minutes, built to run for fifteen people or two thousand.

Operation You Matter Inspiring Minds Bike Build Get On Board Sole Purpose Care Cart Power of reCreation

The reversal — competitors become teachers, and the children arrive as the young scientists.

What it is

Inspiring Minds is a give-back experience with a twist most people never see coming. Your team solves an industry-themed science mystery to open a locked object — then the message inside reveals the real mission: children are arriving as the young scientists, and your people spend the back half of the program making someone else the one who discovers something. Competitors become teachers in the space of one sentence. It runs as one ninety-minute program in three industry variations, plus a hands-on build-and-place format, and scales from a single executive pod to a two-thousand-person general session.

The name is not only about the children. The adults are the heroes of this story — and they leave inspired by the young minds they came to inspire.

Why it lands

The reversal is the whole point.

Most corporate experiences ask people to perform for each other. This one asks them to make someone else the point — then hands them the most reliably inspiring thing there is.

Competitors become teachers

Twenty minutes spent trying to win flips into thirty-five spent helping a child discover. Nobody predicts it, and nobody forgets it.

An hour that beats any keynote

An eleven-year-old genuinely excited about what they just found does something to a person no stage ever has.

Built to scale, not to thin out

One repeatable pod is the unit. Run one for an offsite or three hundred on a convention floor — the experience never weakens as headcount grows.

It keeps teaching

Every child leaves with a resettable kit and a challenge to run on someone else. A corporate afternoon becomes a term of science.

The ninety minutes

One arc, identical at every size.

The same six beats run whether it’s one pod or hundreds — because pods run at the same time, a two-thousand-person session still finishes in ninety minutes. This is the part we’ve already proven, and the structure we don’t rebuild for anyone.

1
0:00 – 0:05 · The mission

Mystery

The locked object is introduced and nothing else is explained. Five teams take five cases off the table. No lecture. Just a clock.

2
0:05 – 0:25 · Investigate

Discovery

Twenty minutes, phones encouraged. The prompts point toward the answer without ever giving it — each team becomes the only expert on its station.

3
0:25 – 0:30 · Converge

The opening

Five separate discoveries become one combination — and one piece is deliberately missing. The room supplies it together. The object opens.

4
0:30 – 0:35 · The reversal

Prepare to inspire

Inside is a rolled message: special guests are arriving, and your real challenge is to inspire a young mind — in five minutes. Competitors become teachers.

5
0:35 – 1:10 · Inspire

The young scientists

One child joins each team of three. The child does the experiment; the adults build the conditions for discovery — the hardest, most revealing thing they’ll do all day. Then each child presents what they found.

6
1:10 – 1:30 · Continue

The second reveal

Every child receives their own locked object — already locked, combination withheld. Solve it, reset it, and build a mystery for someone else.

The rules we don’t bend: no lecture before the mystery, physical objects over screens, the child manipulates the materials and the adult never takes them back, the reveal reframes rather than concludes — and the take-home object is resettable. A souvenir ends the program; a resettable one multiplies it.

Three variations · chosen by industry

Same program. The science on the table is yours.

The engine never changes — mystery, investigation, convergence, reversal, teaching, continuation. What varies is the subject, the artifacts, and the form the lock takes, so the discovery belongs to your people’s world.

Variation I

Secrets Through Time

Security · Technology · Financial services · Defense

For thousands of years people have asked the same five questions: how do I hide information, rearrange it, disguise it, move it across distance, and recover what someone else has protected? The people in the room solve those problems for a living — invisible ink, a scytale, a cipher wheel, a signal lamp, a code to break. Quiet and table-based: the most scalable of the three, from a boardroom to a ballroom of hundreds.

The lockA six-letter cryptex — five letters earned, the sixth guessed by the room.
Variation II

Trace Evidence

Healthcare · Life sciences · Legal · Insurance · Audit

Every contact leaves a trace. Five teams each get one thread from the same incident — a smudged print, an ink sample, a fiber, an impression, two accounts that can’t both be true — and none resolves alone. Nothing here is about crime; the discipline is noticing, then refusing to fall in love with the first hypothesis. It’s the closest of the three to what a diagnostician, underwriter or auditor actually does.

The lockA sealed evidence case under a six-letter seal. Break the seal, not the case.
Variation III

The Long Current

Energy · Utilities · Manufacturing · Logistics · Telecom

Two hundred years ago, moving a force from one place to another was the hardest problem in the world. Five teams work the discoveries that solved it — charge, circuit, magnetism, motion, signal — each a thing that lights, spins, moves, or stubbornly does not. The loudest and most visual of the three, and the best choice for a large room or a business measured in things that move.

The lockA circuit box that opens only when the loop is closed — the last connection made by hand, joining two teams.

Choosing a variation: match the subject to what your people already respect. Security, software and finance take Secrets Through Time; anyone whose job is diagnosis, evidence or judgement takes Trace Evidence; anyone who builds, powers or moves things takes The Long Current. When a team is genuinely mixed, Secrets Through Time travels furthest — and a bespoke fourth subject costs a materials list, not a new program.

Another way to run it · Build & place

A hands-on build that keeps teaching.

Same DNA, different hands. In this format, your team builds real STEM learning machines — solar-and-water powered — alongside local kids, then discovers the twist: each team teaches a child how the machine they built actually works. The machines don’t go home with anyone. They’re placed with a school or community-garden partner, where a teacher uses them with a new class every year.

  • Built, not watched. Kids assemble alongside your team from the start — hand tools only, a fit for an engineer-minded room.
  • A surprise teach-back. Teams are told the machines simply need finishing — then learn children are arriving, with minutes to prepare to teach one.
  • A give-back that lasts. Each machine becomes a permanent teaching tool, touching hundreds of kids the team will never meet.
  • An optional 30-day challenge. One tiny shared habit per person over SMS turns the day into a month the whole team wins together.
What actually gets given

The give-back scales with the room.

Every pod of fifteen participants means five more children with kits of their own — so a general session of a thousand people is a thousand-participant event and a three-hundred-child event at the same time. That’s the number to put in front of a sponsor.

Every child leaves with a kit

A reusable field case holding their own locked object — already locked, combination withheld. Inside: five secrets, one per station. Solve them, work out the last one, open it. With it travels a field book that rebuilds each experiment from household objects, and a challenge to run on somebody else. Its first page reads: scientists don’t just collect answers, they collect questions.

Every partner leaves with a collection

The children in the room aren’t the only beneficiaries. Each partner school or youth organization receives a classroom collection — additional locked objects, the science behind each one, the station kits, consumables to run the sequence through the year, and a facilitator guide. Larger events fund collections for several partner organizations at once.

The instruction that matters

The note inside the child’s lock: “You cracked the code. But that wasn’t the real mission. The real mission is what happens next.” Reset the lock. Choose a new combination. Build a mystery for a brother, a friend, a classroom. Inspire another mind.

For planners

Operating requirements & scale.

One pod is fifteen participants, five children, five station tables and one locked object. Every configuration below is that unit multiplied — and because pods run simultaneously, duration never changes with size.

FormatParticipantsPodsChildrenRoom & staffing
Leadership offsite15–301–25–10Boardroom. One lead facilitator.
Department day45–1203–815–40Single ballroom or office floor. One lead, one facilitator per two pods.
Conference breakout150–45010–3050–150Ballroom, rounds of ten. Stage lead on mic, roaming facilitators, per-pod captains briefed in advance.
General session500–2,00033–133165–665Main hall with AV and countdown clock. Stage-led timing, zone captains, multiple partner organizations.

Fixed at every size: ninety minutes, three adults to one child, five stations per pod, one locked object per pod, and the reveal happens once for the whole room at minute thirty. Lead time: roughly three weeks to around ten pods; six to eight weeks beyond that, for kit production and partner recruitment. Young scientists are approximately ages 11–13, one per team of three; partner organizations coordinate arrival, consent and chaperones, timed to minute thirty-five regardless of scale.

Measure it twice

Was the child inspired — and was the adult beside them?

People remember the moment they found out they could cause that — a young person discovering something in front of them, because of them. That is the shift, and it is why the program exists.

Questions, answered

Inspiring Minds FAQs

What is Inspiring Minds? +

A give-back team building experience. Your team solves an industry-themed science mystery to open a locked object — then the message inside reveals the real mission: children are arriving as the young scientists, and your people spend the rest of the program helping them discover something. Competitors become teachers, and the adults leave inspired by the young minds they came to inspire.

How many people can take part? +

From 15 to 2,000. The program is built out of one repeatable unit — a pod of fifteen participants with five young scientists — so it runs for a single executive team or a full conference general session. Because pods run simultaneously, it still finishes in ninety minutes at any size.

How long does it take? +

Ninety minutes, at every group size. Pods run at the same time rather than in sequence, so a two-thousand-person general session finishes in the same ninety minutes as a single-pod leadership offsite.

What are the three variations? +

The engine never changes; the subject on the table does. Secrets Through Time (codes and ciphers) suits security, technology, financial services and defense. Trace Evidence (forensic noticing) suits healthcare, life sciences, legal, insurance and audit. The Long Current (electricity and motion) suits energy, utilities, manufacturing, logistics and telecom. There’s also a hands-on build-and-place format where teams build real learning machines with the children.

What do the children receive? +

Every child leaves with a kit — a reusable field case holding their own locked object, already locked with the combination withheld, plus a field book that rebuilds each experiment from household objects. Partner schools and youth organizations receive a classroom collection: additional locked objects, station kits, a facilitator guide and consumables to run the sequence through the year. Every pod of fifteen participants means five more children with kits of their own.

How far in advance should we book? +

Roughly three weeks for events up to about ten pods, and six to eight weeks beyond that, for kit production and partner recruitment. Tell us your date, group size and city and we’ll send a tailored proposal, usually within a business day.
